title: Like, want, and need
goal: Saying what you like, want, and need — and meeting a sentence pattern where the thing you like becomes the subject, not you.
bekal: say you like or dislike something, in two different ways
say you want, need, and have to
use feeling adjectives that agree with the speaker's gender

dialogs.title: خبرې اترې — د چای پر مهال

notes: Pashto has **two** ways to say you like something, and both are correct. The first, and by far the more common, is **ما ته ... خوښېږي** — literally "to me ... is pleasing". In this sentence the subject is **the thing that's liked**, not the person.
The second is **زه ... خوښوم**, with the usual word order, as in English. It's correct and understood, but sounds a little more formal or stronger — closer to "I'm fond of" than to "I like".

⚠️ Because the thing liked is the subject, the verb agrees with it. ما ته سړې اوبه ډېرې **خوښېږي** uses the plural because اوبه is always plural. If you forget and use the singular, you're still understood, but it sounds shaky.

The word راته means "to me", a short form of ما ته. Its siblings: **درته** (to you), **ورته** (to him/her). You'll hear these three little words dozens of times a day, and unit 17 covers them in full.
The phrase پکار دي means "needed", and it works exactly like خوښېږي: the thing needed is the subject. The sentence is ما ته اوبه **پکار دي**, literally "to me water needed is".

Note once more that تږی (thirsty) and وږی (hungry) behave like ordinary adjectives: زه تږی یم. Pashto doesn't use the "to me" pattern for these two — and here it's closer to English than Persian or Urdu are.

grammars.title: The verb خوښېدل: the thing liked becomes the subject
body: The order is: the person who likes takes **ته**, then the thing liked, then the verb **خوښېږي**, which agrees with that thing. This sentence pattern has no everyday match in English and is best memorized as a whole.
English has something similar in *it pleases me*, and Spanish uses it every day in *me gusta*. If you've studied Spanish, this pattern will feel familiar.

grammars.title: Want, need, must, can
body: Four ideas that are easy to mix up have clearly different forms in Pashto. Note that **غواړم** and **باید** use the usual order with زه, while **پکار دي** uses the ته pattern, like خوښېږي.
⚠️ The verb after غواړم takes the **base form**, not the form with a personal ending: زه تلل غواړم, not زه ځم غواړم. The base form is the one ending in ـل.

sections.title: Feelings, states, and how to say them

blocks.text: Feeling adjectives in Pashto agree with the gender of the person saying them. The second column below is what a man says, the third what a woman says — and the choice depends on who is speaking, not who is listening.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Two words for "hot" you mustn't mix up
items: The word **ګرم** *garm* means hot in temperature: چای ګرم دی (the tea is hot), زه ګرم یم (I'm hot).
The word **تېز** *tez* means spicy, and also fast or sharp: مرچ تېز دی (the chili is spicy), موټر تېز دی (the car is fast).
English uses "hot" for both temperature and spice; Pashto keeps them apart, and uses تېز for spice, speed, and a sharp knife all at once. Context separates them, and nobody ever gets confused.
The opposites: **یخ** *yakh* (icy, ice-cold) and **سوړ** *soṛ* (cool, ordinary cold). Cold water is سړې اوبه, not یخې اوبه — unless you really want ice water.

blocks.title: What people usually like, and what they usually ask
items: The safest opening question: **تاسو ته افغانستان څنګه ښکاري؟** *tāso ta Afghānistān tsənga ṣkārī* — "how do you find Afghanistan?".
About food: **تاسو ته کوم خواړه خوښېږي؟** — "which food do you like?". An answer that always pleases the host: **ما ته قابلي پلو ډېر خوښېږي**.
About places: **تاسو ته کابل خوښېږي؟** — "do you like Kabul?". If you don't have an opinion yet, answer **لا زه نوی یم** *lā zə naway yəm*, "I'm still new here".
⚠️ Avoid giving opinions on politics, religion, or ethnicity in your first weeks. Not because it's dangerous, but because your vocabulary isn't yet enough to fix any misunderstanding that comes up.
